segments.title: Old power technologies endured through better engineering
segments.body: A viewer traces rotary steam devices to ancient Greece, large-scale windmill development to medieval and early-modern Europe, and industrial water power to mills and pumps. The examples support a wider point: technological progress often makes familiar processes more capable instead of replacing them with wholly new principles. Modern nuclear stations still use steam to drive turbines, while wind turbines and hydroelectric plants refine older ways of extracting energy from moving air and water. These technologies place nineteenth-century industrial power within a much longer engineering history.

evidence.note: The comment and response connect ancient steam devices, windmills, water power, and modern energy systems through continuing engineering improvement.

segments.summary: Ancient steam demonstrations and centuries of wind and water machinery show how technological change often improves established principles.

segments.title: Why converting line-of-battle ships into ironclads was costly
segments.body: Existing ships could be razeed and considered for ironclad conversion, but the expense quickly undermined the apparent savings. Adding armour was not a simple refit because the hull, stability, propulsion, and internal arrangement all had to support a different kind of fighting ship. The work could become nearly as demanding as a new design. That cost helps explain why navies often preferred new construction while large wooden ships remained on hand.

evidence.note: The question asks about ironclad conversion, and the answer stresses the expense despite razee options.

segments.summary: Armouring a first-class line-of-battle ship was technically possible but rarely economical.
segments.question: Could a first-class line-of-battle ship be converted into an ironclad at acceptable cost?
segments.answerShort: It was possible and sometimes considered, but the conversion was usually expensive enough to make navies hesitate.

segments.title: Coal bunkers offered conditional protection
segments.body: Designers placed coal around vital spaces because a filled bunker could act as a barrier and reduce the volume available for floodwater. Coal occupied much of a bunker's volume, so a damaged full bunker admitted less water than an empty compartment. The protection changed as the ship steamed, however, because a distant-station cruiser consumed the very material forming the barrier. An empty bunker could leave air space and hazardous coal dust where protection was expected. Fuel state therefore determined how much protection, flood control, and stability the arrangement could provide.

evidence.note: The answer describes coal as armour, its flooding benefit, and the limits created by consumption and coal dust.

segments.summary: Coal could absorb damage and limit flooding, but only while the bunker remained full and safely managed.
segments.question: How effective was coal-bunker protection on nominally unarmoured cruisers?
segments.answerShort: Full coal bunkers could provide useful protection and reduce flooding, but that benefit disappeared as fuel was consumed and empty dusty bunkers could add danger.

segments.title: When unprotected cruisers made strategic sense
segments.body: Unprotected cruisers were poor choices for peer fleet combat, but they could serve in piracy suppression, anti-slavery patrols, colonial policing, and showing the flag. Those missions demanded range, presence, and numbers more often than the ability to exchange heavy fire. Three cheaper hulls might keep one ship continuously on station when two more costly protected cruisers were both unavailable for repair or refit. Force readiness depended on the number of ships available, not the specifications of a single hull. An unprotected cruiser could therefore be sensible when its role and likely opposition were tightly defined.

evidence.note: The answer contrasts peer combat with policing roles and explains the availability gained from cheaper ships.

segments.summary: Cheap unprotected cruisers could suit policing and presence missions where numbers and availability mattered more than battle protection.
segments.question: Would an unprotected cruiser be worth building?
segments.answerShort: Yes for low-threat policing and presence roles, especially when low cost buys enough hulls to sustain availability, but not as a peer-war fighting ship.

segments.title: A tiered Royal Navy cruiser force for global commitments
segments.body: Unprotected cruisers provide communications, searches, and day-to-day presence, while protected and armoured cruisers supply escalating combat power behind them. In a pre-radio fleet, numerous small ships could extend search grids, repeat signals, and reveal where heavier forces were needed. A modest station ship also represented the frigates, battleships, and carriers that its navy could send after it. The proposed budget mix keeps much of the expensive force in ordinary while using cheaper ships heavily in peacetime. As war approached, the protected ships would commission and the cruiser network would redistribute for combat, making reserve policy part of force design rather than an afterthought.

evidence.note: The viewer proposes a three-tier cruiser force for British global commitments and pre-radio operations.
The answer connects presence to heavier reinforcement and proposes budget, commission, and reserve proportions.

segments.summary: A viewer's mixed cruiser fleet leads to a discussion of global presence, reinforcement, reserve policy, and wartime mobilization.
segments.question: How should the Royal Navy balance unprotected, protected, and armoured cruisers for worldwide duties?
segments.answerShort: Use numerous cheap cruisers for routine presence, retain protected and armoured ships as reinforcing combat power, and preserve much of the expensive force in reserve until tensions rise.

segments.title: Small purpose-built cruisers versus armed merchant cruisers
segments.body: Small unprotected cruisers could cover anti-slavery patrols, revenue duties, distant stations, and wartime trade protection. A purpose-built naval vessel could remain available without withdrawing a useful merchant hull from commerce at the outbreak of war. Regular orders for these ships could also sustain smaller yards and create local repair capacity in Britain or its colonies. Requisitioned liners, by contrast, imposed exceptionally high fuel and operating costs once taken up from trade. Cruiser procurement therefore affected mobilization planning and the wider industrial economy.

evidence.note: Comments and response compare small cruisers with merchant conversions, including industrial and operating costs.

segments.summary: Small purpose-built cruisers could cover patrol and trade-protection work without removing costly liners from commerce.
segments.question: Why choose a small purpose-built unprotected cruiser over an armed merchant cruiser?
segments.answerShort: It could perform routine naval work economically, support shipbuilding capacity, and remain available without withdrawing an expensive liner from trade.

segments.title: Why unprotected cruisers were often too slow to escape
segments.body: A fast raider could avoid stronger opponents and disrupt trade, but speed cost money in machinery, boilers, and fuel. Navies that economized on armour frequently economized on the propulsion plant as well. The resulting cruiser could neither absorb punishment nor reliably escape a stronger enemy. Its low speed therefore compounded its lack of protection instead of compensating for it. Many ships did not receive every theoretical advantage associated with their design category.

evidence.note: The answer contrasts the ideal fast raider with slow ships produced by low machinery spending.

segments.summary: The ideal commerce raider traded armour for speed, but low-cost procurement often denied unprotected cruisers both.
segments.question: Could unprotected cruisers rely on speed for commerce raiding and survival?
segments.answerShort: In theory, but many were built cheaply with weak machinery, leaving them slow as well as unprotected.

segments.title: How battleship and cruiser design roles diverged
segments.body: The question frames battleships as broad, heavily armoured combatants and cruisers as narrower, faster ships with less protection. That distinction captures the emerging trade between protection, speed, and cruising role. The period resisted such a clean division because some armoured cruisers approached second-class battleship characteristics. USS Maine is offered as a borderline example, along with the assessment that her loss just before the Spanish-American War was probably accidental. Classification followed doctrine and institutional choice as well as dimensions or armour thickness. Applying later categories too rigidly can therefore distort nineteenth-century warship roles.

evidence.note: The exchange discusses armour, speed, hull form, USS Maine, and designs crossing the cruiser-battleship boundary.

segments.summary: Armour, hull form, and speed helped separate battleships from cruisers, though USS Maine and other contemporary designs straddled the boundary.
segments.question: Did armour distribution and hull form create the distinction between battleships and cruisers?
segments.answerShort: They contributed to the divergence, but contemporary designs could blur the line between an armoured cruiser and a second-class battleship.

segments.title: Warrior, Black Prince, and changing warship classifications
segments.body: The claim that the ships simply moved from battleship to armoured-cruiser status by bureaucratic whim does not fit their service history. Warrior and Black Prince entered service as armoured frigates when that term could describe ships near the top of the naval hierarchy. They occupied an early ironclad center point from which battleship, armoured-cruiser, and protected-cruiser design strands later diverged. The ships did not physically transform when the vocabulary changed, but the surrounding fleet and meaning of each category did. Their reclassification therefore records an evolving naval system rather than a clerk casually redrawing a label.

evidence.note: The answer corrects the battleship claim and places the ships at the branching point of ironclad classifications.
Dr. Clarke explains why classification was more than an arbitrary bureaucratic stroke of the pen.

segments.summary: Warrior and Black Prince began as armoured frigates at a moment when later battleship and cruiser categories had not fully separated.
segments.question: Were Warrior and Black Prince battleships later reclassified as armoured cruisers?
segments.answerShort: No; they were armoured frigates from an early ironclad era whose design position later overlapped categories that had evolved around them.

segments.title: Why lightly protected cruisers became eggshells armed with hammers
segments.body: A viewer describes lightly protected cruisers as eggshells armed with hammers, capturing the imbalance between their weapons and survivability. Limited gunnery accuracy initially reduced the chance of a damaging hit at distance. Crews often answered that problem by closing the range until their fire became effective. The same move made the enemy's weapons more likely to penetrate the cruiser in return. Tactical practice could therefore expose the protection compromise that made the design affordable.

evidence.note: The comment describes eggshells armed with hammers, and Dr. Clarke explains that poor accuracy encouraged ships to close into more dangerous ranges.

segments.summary: Powerful guns and weak protection made early cruisers especially vulnerable once poor long-range accuracy drove them into close action.

segments.title: Why sailing rigs lost value on steam cruisers
segments.body: Sail retained value while engines and fuel supply were unreliable, but that advantage declined as steam plants and coaling networks improved. A sailing rig was not free endurance because masts, rigging, and working space constrained arcs of fire and the placement of machinery. Designers first had to fit the propulsion systems needed to move the hull and then accommodate the sailing plant around them. Weapons, stores, and crew spaces inherited the remaining compromises. The transition from sail to steam was a problem of whole-ship arrangement as much as a choice between power sources.

evidence.note: The answer connects sail's declining value to engineering reliability, coal access, and internal design priorities.

segments.summary: Reliable engines and worldwide coal access turned sailing rigs from useful redundancy into a constraint on machinery and weapons layout.
segments.question: Was a full sailing rig more valuable on an unprotected cruiser than on a protected cruiser?
segments.answerShort: Its value depended less on armour than on engine reliability and coal access; as both improved, rigging increasingly obstructed machinery and armament layout.

segments.title: Freeboard and habitability could make a cruiser a better flagship
segments.body: A viewer argues that these large cruisers offered enough freeboard and internal volume to serve as practical peacetime flagships. Low-freeboard ironclads in the Mediterranean might possess heavier combat power but offered poor accommodation for an admiral and staff. Better living and working space mattered for health, administration, and sustained command even when it did not appear in a gun-and-armour comparison. The flag could transfer to a stronger ship when war began. Habitability and command function could give an expensive cruiser value beyond its place in the battle line.

evidence.note: The comment favors a high-freeboard cruiser as an admiral's peacetime ship and contrasts its accommodation with Mediterranean ironclads.

segments.summary: A roomy high-freeboard cruiser could support an admiral and staff more comfortably than a cramped low-freeboard ironclad.

segments.title: Why so few early warships survived as museums
segments.body: A remark about a French 74-gun ship leads into why societies often scrapped vessels that later generations would treasure. Keeping a large wooden warship demanded money, space, and maintenance after its military usefulness had faded. Naval institutions were usually oriented toward replacement technology and saw little reason to preserve an obsolete burden. That calculation differs from the modern desire for tangible links to the past. Survival as a museum ship reflects later cultural priorities as much as a vessel's original historical importance.

evidence.note: The discussion moves from a lost French 74 to preservation costs, future-oriented institutions, and historical memory.

segments.summary: The loss of potential museum ships reflects cost, faith in newer technology, and changing public attachment to tangible history.

segments.title: Wampanoag, fast steam cruisers, and engineering politics
segments.body: The viewer distinguishes successful Wampanoag-class performance from several failed fast-cruiser experiments and supplies evidence on speed, range, coal economy, and habitability. Wampanoag met demanding trial figures, while other Civil War designs damaged the reputation of the entire program. Proposed deck changes also show that a technically promising ship could still require substantial correction before routine service. The stronger case for Wampanoag still leaves Benjamin Isherwood's political weakness after the war. Engineering brilliance alone could not secure funding once emergency conditions ended, so institutional rivalry shaped which technical lessons survived.

evidence.note: The comment details Civil War fast-cruiser designs, Wampanoag's performance, storage, and proposed deck modification.
Dr. Clarke explains the continuing technical problems and Isherwood's inability to adapt politically after the war.

segments.summary: American Civil War cruiser trials show how machinery performance, design rivalry, and political skill shaped which innovations survived.

segments.title: Pacocha and the difference between survival and victory
segments.body: Both sides remained afloat, and Huáscar withdrew after nightfall, which can make the engagement look tactically indecisive. Sources disagree on whether the British projectiles count as armour-piercing, semi-armour-piercing, or neither, so that ammunition claim remains bracketed. The clearer measure is the mission assigned to the Royal Navy force. The British intended to blockade, contain, or destroy the Peruvian ironclad, and Huáscar escaped. Damage inflicted without achieving that purpose did not satisfy a navy whose institutional standard demanded decisive success. Battle assessment must therefore distinguish tactical exchanges from operational objectives, which is why the Royal Navy treated the outcome as a lesson.

evidence.note: The challenge raises Huáscar's escape, disputed shell classifications, and whether the action was a draw.
The answer defines the British objective and explains why failing to sink or contain Huáscar was treated as a loss.

segments.summary: Pacocha counts as a British operational failure because Huáscar escaped instead of being destroyed or contained.
segments.question: Was the Battle of Pacocha really a British loss if Huáscar withdrew and neither side was sunk?
segments.answerShort: Yes in operational terms, because the Royal Navy failed to sink or contain Huáscar and therefore did not achieve the objective it had set.

segments.title: Russian naval institutions needed sustained investment
segments.body: Russian sailors and designers were not inherently incompetent, and Russian institutions could produce capable people and interesting work. The deeper problem was that schools, accommodation, logistics, and organizational systems were created and then allowed to decay. Establishing an academy or base once did not preserve its buildings, staff, doctrine, or accumulated knowledge. Naval capability depended on continuing funding, maintenance, and access to the information personnel needed. Repeated failure was an institutional-sustainment problem rather than a national character trait.

evidence.note: Dr. Clarke separates Russian people from failures of support and access to necessary institutions.
The answer describes neglected educational infrastructure and states that organization is an ongoing investment.

segments.summary: The Russian Navy's recurring failures reflected neglected institutions and infrastructure rather than an absence of capable people or ideas.
segments.question: Was the Russian Navy simply incompetent and incapable of learning?
segments.answerShort: No; it could create strong institutions and designs, but leadership repeatedly failed to sustain the infrastructure, education, and organization needed to preserve capability.

segments.title: Britain, Russia, and the strategic problem of Afghanistan
segments.body: A comment frames the Russian Empire as a long-term threat to British India. Britain and Russia repeatedly tried to work through Afghanistan, while direct involvement ignored the country's political difficulty. The proposed approach is to support a tolerable local partner, supply weapons, and let that partner govern while investing in infrastructure such as a railway. The Great Game aside connects imperial rivalry to proxy strategy, transport, and state capacity.

evidence.note: The exchange links Russian pressure on British India with intervention in Afghanistan, support for a local partner, and railway investment.

segments.summary: Anglo-Russian rivalry over British India leads to a compact argument for local partners and infrastructure in Afghanistan.

segments.title: A submerged armour belt was not intentional torpedo protection
segments.body: The question jokes that General-Admiral's submerged belt accidentally became an early anti-torpedo system. Armour below the surface might resist some underwater damage, so the idea is not entirely absurd as a description of the physical effect. It was not, however, a purpose-designed torpedo-defence system. The belt had settled away from the waterline it was meant to protect because the ship displaced more than intended. British armoured cruisers suffered the same dangerous consequence, so the example concerns weight growth and stability rather than accidental innovation.

evidence.note: The exchange considers torpedo effects and notes both Russian and British belts settling below the waterline.

segments.summary: An armour belt settling below the waterline could offer limited underwater resistance, but it exposed a design and displacement failure.
segments.question: Did an armour belt ending up below the waterline create an early form of torpedo defence?
segments.answerShort: Only incidentally and imperfectly; the belt might resist some underwater damage, but its submerged position reflected a serious protection problem shared by several navies.

segments.title: Russian warship delays and displacement growth
segments.body: Imperial Russian designers sometimes got the concept right, yet slow construction could make the completed ship obsolete. One contemporary criticism held that an 8,000-ton design could emerge above 9,000 or even 10,000 tons. Schedule delay, displacement growth, and cost overruns therefore eroded the value of an otherwise promising design. The nearby submerged-belt problem shows how excess weight could also defeat the intended protection scheme.

evidence.note: The comment and response describe Russian designs becoming obsolete during construction and exceeding intended displacement, schedule, and budget.

segments.summary: Promising Russian warship designs could arrive obsolete, overweight, late, and over budget.

segments.title: A balanced hypothetical redesign of General-Admiral
segments.body: A viewer sketches a successor or reconstruction with twin shafts, greater speed, at least the same range, and a centreline battery of eight-inch or larger guns. The armour belt would have to remain above the waterline, while a less rounded bow would improve behaviour in Atlantic seas. Each proposal addresses a different weakness: propulsion redundancy, speed, firing arcs, protection placement, or seakeeping. Taken together, they show why repairing one visible defect would not have made General-Admiral a balanced cruiser. The proposal remains a retrospective design exercise; Russia did not build it as a programme.

evidence.note: The viewer proposes twin shafts, higher speed, centreline guns, an armour belt above water, and a more seaworthy bow.

segments.summary: A viewer's hypothetical redesign shows that General-Admiral needed coordinated changes to machinery, armament, armour, and seakeeping.

segments.title: Unproven weapons depend on the enemy behaving as expected
segments.body: A comment about uncertain technologies leads to the Royal Navy's early Second World War rocket-propelled anti-aircraft munitions. The system was justified against level-flying bombers and might have performed adequately in that narrow engagement. Actual attackers did not cooperate with the assumed flight profile, so the weapon's operating concept collapsed even though the underlying technology could function. It was quickly abandoned while successful wartime weapons received far more attention afterward. The example shows that combat effectiveness depends on enemy behavior and doctrine as much as laboratory promise.

evidence.note: The comment frames the uncertainty surrounding new military technologies before combat.
Dr. Clarke uses failed naval anti-aircraft rockets to show how operational assumptions can invalidate a design.

segments.summary: Promising technology can fail because its target and combat conditions differ from the scenario used to justify it.

segments.title: HMS Shannon and the return of the ram concept
segments.body: The prompt argues that Shannon was laid out around ramming at the expense of general duties. Her concentration of forward fire and protection encouraged a head-on closing action rather than flexible cruiser employment. She was not completed with the intended ram, so the tactical concept remained only partially embodied in the ship. Had Shannon proved successful, designers might have treated her as a precedent for HMS Polyphemus and other vessels built around the attack approach. The unsuccessful design still reveals a possible evolutionary path toward later ram ships.

evidence.note: The exchange connects Shannon's intended ramming role to the later Polyphemus concept.

segments.summary: Shannon's forward-fighting concept suggests a possible design path toward later ram-oriented warships such as Polyphemus.
segments.question: Was HMS Shannon designed too narrowly around ramming?
segments.answerShort: Her layout reflected a forward-closing concept even though she lacked the intended ram, and success might have encouraged a direct line toward later ram ships such as Polyphemus.

segments.title: Why navies might hide a failed warship
segments.body: A viewer explains why a navy might quietly deploy a disappointing vessel far from scrutiny instead of publicly admitting failure. Openly acknowledging a bad design could weaken confidence in future appropriations and expose the officers or officials who had supported it. Promotion, honours, and factional rivalry gave individuals reasons to minimize the mistake. A distant station also offered a chance to obtain some practical service from the hull without testing it against a first-rate opponent. Institutional incentives could therefore keep a failed procurement decision alive after its technical weaknesses were understood.

evidence.note: The comment links distant deployment to confidence, future funding, careers, and naval factions.

segments.summary: Sending an unsuccessful ship to a distant station could protect public confidence, budgets, and the careers tied to its design.

segments.title: Trafalgar versus Lissa in Shannon's forward-fire layout
segments.body: A head-on approach that breaks the enemy line and fires while passing differs from the later fixation on Lissa's 1866 ramming example. Trafalgar supplied an image of charging through the formation and engaging as the ship crossed the line. Lissa encouraged a stronger expectation that the ram itself could decide the action. Shannon's forward weapons supported the first concept even though her design also pointed toward the second. The ship sits between age-of-sail line-breaking imagery and later purpose-built ram tactics.

evidence.note: The answer contrasts Trafalgar line-breaking fire with Lissa-inspired ramming and applies the distinction to Shannon.

segments.summary: Shannon's arrangement drew on a Trafalgar-style line-breaking attack, while later ram designs more directly reflected Lissa.
segments.question: Did HMS Shannon's tactical layout owe more to Trafalgar or to the Battle of Lissa?
segments.answerShort: More to Trafalgar's line-breaking approach; the stronger Lissa-style ramming influence appears in later designs, though Shannon may foreshadow them.

segments.title: Shannon's forward armour left a shell trap
segments.body: The viewer points out that fragments striking the armoured face still needed somewhere to go and that an enemy could hit the unprotected structure around it. Shannon's armour concentrated protection on the forward target presented during her intended attack. Side guns, surrounding structure, and much of the hull remained exposed to off-angle fire. Even a hit on the armour could throw dangerous fragments into adjacent spaces. Shannon was a ship of contradictions: the protection served a narrow tactical idea while leaving much of the fighting ship vulnerable.

evidence.note: The question identifies the shell trap, and Dr. Clarke agrees that Shannon's protection embodied contradictory choices.

segments.summary: Shannon's armour protected a chosen forward arc but left guns and adjacent structure dangerously exposed to fragments and off-angle hits.
segments.question: Did HMS Shannon's armour create a shell trap and leave the rest of the ship exposed?
segments.answerShort: Yes; the armour covered a limited forward target while fragments, side guns, and lightly protected structure remained serious vulnerabilities.

segments.title: Why an undersized shell could destroy its gun
segments.body: Without a proper fit or effective wadding, the smaller projectile could oscillate and corkscrew rather than travel cleanly down the barrel. The extra clearance allowed it to yaw and strike the bore instead of remaining aligned with the gun's axis. In the worst case the shell could lock against the barrel while propellant gases continued to build behind it. The result was a burst gun and lethal danger to the crew. An engineering report's vocabulary for progressively worse motion gives the amusing question a concrete connection to ammunition compatibility and ordnance safety.

evidence.note: The answer explains bore instability, jamming, gun failure, and the terminology used in an engineering report.

segments.summary: A nine-inch projectile fired from a ten-inch gun could yaw inside the bore, jam, and burst the weapon and its crew.
segments.question: What happens if a nine-inch shell is loaded into a ten-inch gun?
segments.answerShort: The poor fit can make the projectile yaw and jam in the bore, potentially bursting the gun and killing its crew.

segments.title: Learning from a failed warship before combat exposes it
segments.body: A viewer proposes repurposing an uneconomic vessel and commissioning an inquiry into what went wrong. Depot or accommodation duty could preserve limited value without pretending that the ship remained an effective combatant. A formal study could identify design-process failures before they were repeated in another class. The cost of that investigation was small compared with another failed ship or the reputational damage of discovering the weakness in combat. The logic is sound, though political incentives often resist such candid institutional learning.

evidence.note: The comment proposes repurposing and investigation, and the response notes that politics is less level-headed.

segments.summary: An unsuccessful ship can become a depot or training asset while a formal study protects the navy from repeating the design failure.

segments.title: An American modernization plan for HMS Shannon
segments.body: The proposed refit substitutes a four-bladed disconnecting screw for Shannon's inefficient propeller so that she could steam better without sacrificing sailing performance. A unified battery of modern rifles would replace her mismatched guns and simplify the fighting arrangement. The proposal is judged against the weak U.S. fleet of 1881 rather than against the strongest Royal Navy ships. In a navy still dominated by wooden corvettes, gunboats, and monitors, even this flawed British cruiser could have supplied a credible high-seas armoured hull. The comparison also shows how Chilean, Argentine, and Brazilian acquisitions shaped North American assessments of naval adequacy.

evidence.note: The comment compares U.S. failures with Shannon and specifies machinery and armament changes for an American purchase.

segments.summary: A hypothetical 1881 U.S. purchase would replace Shannon's screw and mixed armament to create a credible high-seas armoured ship.

segments.title: Secondary roles for an obsolete or unsuccessful warship
segments.body: The closing response lists practical ways to extract value from a vessel that no longer merits front-line service. A sound hull might train crews, test guns, patrol fisheries, carry stores, house personnel or prisoners, or serve as a target. None of those duties required pretending that the ship could still defeat a modern opponent. The alternatives separate the sunk cost of the hull from the narrower question of whether it remained safe and useful for auxiliary work. This is a compact example of matching residual capability to a secondary mission instead of allowing prestige to dictate employment.

evidence.note: The transcript lists training, testing, patrol, accommodation, transport, prison, and target uses.

segments.summary: A ship that could not be sold might still serve in training, trials, patrol, accommodation, transport, or target duties.
